report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Spatial epidemic models estimate disease transmission counts between populations using human mobility data, but location-to-location transmission is rarely observed directly.
To address this gap, we develop mutation-counting methods to infer transmission structure from viral genetic variation measured in wastewater.
In epidemic simulations with known transmission networks, our primary estimator robustly recovers spatial structure under realistic mutation-detection limits.

Applied to spatiotemporal SARS-CoV-2 wastewater data from Austria, the method reveals strong seasonal reorganization, with inferred transmission becoming more geographically localized in winter and more dispersed in summer.
We further identify locations with systematically higher or lower connectivity than expected from commuting, with temporal changes coinciding with regional restrictions, reopening and tourism.

We then test whether such inference remains possible across national borders, recovering coherent spatial structure and temporal variation in connectivity between Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

These results establish wastewater sequence data as a promising complement to mobility data for monitoring spatial transmission and detecting changes in epidemic spread associated with seasonality and interventions.

Network epidemic models provide a natural framework for representing the spatial spread of infectious diseases, with mobility, commuting and contact data commonly used to define connections between locations [1, 2, 3, 4].
text.formatted: Network epidemic models provide a natural framework for representing the spatial spread of infectious diseases, with mobility, commuting and contact data commonly used to define connections between locations <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: However, such data capture opportunities for movement and interaction rather than the transmission events realized during an epidemic.

The network of realized transmissions may therefore differ substantially from that implied by mobility and contact data, as transmission also depends on the nature and intensity of interactions, the infection and immunity status of individuals, and stochastic infection events [5].
text.formatted: The network of realized transmissions may therefore differ substantially from that implied by mobility and contact data, as transmission also depends on the nature and intensity of interactions, the infection and immunity status of individuals, and stochastic infection events <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Since location-to-location transmission is rarely observed directly, these differences remain difficult to quantify empirically [6].
text.formatted: Since location-to-location transmission is rarely observed directly, these differences remain difficult to quantify empirically <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Here, we show how wastewater sequence data can be used to estimate spatial transmission structure from the genetic variation of a pathogen.
A growing body of research has used genomic data to estimate spatial transmission patterns.
Phylodynamic approaches reconstruct phylogenetic relationships between sampled genomes and use geographic annotations to infer migration or transmission between populations [7, 8, 9].
text.formatted: Phylodynamic approaches reconstruct phylogenetic relationships between sampled genomes and use geographic annotations to infer migration or transmission between populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: More recently, direct methods have been developed to infer transmission patterns without phylogenetic reconstruction.

Spatial transmission between populations has been inferred from identical or closely related clinical consensus sequences [10, 11], while machine-learning approaches have been used to identify the spatial scales of interactions associated with viral genetic structure [12].
text.formatted: Spatial transmission between populations has been inferred from identical or closely related clinical consensus sequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>, while machine-learning approaches have been used to identify the spatial scales of interactions associated with viral genetic structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: At the individual level, clinical sequences have been combined with observed or modelled contact-network information to reconstruct transmission structure [13, 14].
text.formatted: At the individual level, clinical sequences have been combined with observed or modelled contact-network information to reconstruct transmission structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14]</ref>.

text.text: Genetic variation has also been used to identify superspreading events and infer subsequent changes in epidemic behaviour that can alter spatial transmission patterns [15].
text.formatted: Genetic variation has also been used to identify superspreading events and infer subsequent changes in epidemic behaviour that can alter spatial transmission patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: However, these approaches generally rely on individual-level genomes obtained through clinical surveillance, which can introduce sampling biases arising from factors such as socioeconomic inequalities in testing uptake and geographic disparities in sequencing capacity [16, 17].
text.formatted: However, these approaches generally rely on individual-level genomes obtained through clinical surveillance, which can introduce sampling biases arising from factors such as socioeconomic inequalities in testing uptake and geographic disparities in sequencing capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref>.

text.text: Wastewater surveillance offers a complementary population-level approach that can mitigate sampling biases associated with clinical testing by providing broad coverage at relatively low per-capita costs [18, 19].
text.formatted: Wastewater surveillance offers a complementary population-level approach that can mitigate sampling biases associated with clinical testing by providing broad coverage at relatively low per-capita costs <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19]</ref>.

text.text: Contact patterns between locations give rise to realized transmission through epidemic spread, which is reflected in pathogen genetic variation.
Wastewater sequencing provides an incomplete observation of this variation because of withincatchment mixing, incomplete sampling and detection limits.
We infer estimated transmission matrices (ETMs) from these wastewater mutation observations.
In synthetic experiments, ETMs can be compared directly with the known realized transmission matrix and underlying contact structure.

In empirical data, ETMs are compared with independent mobility and commuting data to identify both broad similarities in spatial transmission structure and departures from mobility-based expectations.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, wastewater monitoring expanded rapidly, with national and regional programs established in many countries to monitor SARS-CoV-2 circulation at the population level [20].
text.formatted: During the COVID-19 pandemic, wastewater monitoring expanded rapidly, with national and regional programs established in many countries to monitor SARS-CoV-2 circulation at the population level <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: While many surveillance programs initially focused on measuring viral concentrations to track community prevalence, wastewater sequencing was also integrated into several programs to monitor SARS-CoV-2 lineage dynamics over time and across locations [19, 21, 22, 23, 24].
text.formatted: While many surveillance programs initially focused on measuring viral concentrations to track community prevalence, wastewater sequencing was also integrated into several programs to monitor SARS-CoV-2 lineage dynamics over time and across locations <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24]</ref>.

text.text: In addition to monitoring circulating lineages, wastewater sequencing can capture viral genetic diversity from multiple infections within a catchment, including those missed by clinical surveillance [19, 22].
text.formatted: In addition to monitoring circulating lineages, wastewater sequencing can capture viral genetic diversity from multiple infections within a catchment, including those missed by clinical surveillance <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref>.

text.text: This diversity can also provide information about local epidemic activity beyond viral concentration measurements, as demonstrated by its association with community COVID-19 incidence [25].
text.formatted: This diversity can also provide information about local epidemic activity beyond viral concentration measurements, as demonstrated by its association with community COVID-19 incidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, wastewater sequence data pose several challenges [26].
text.formatted: At the same time, wastewater sequence data pose several challenges <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: Each sample contains genetic material shed by many infected individuals, making it difficult to determine which mutations occur together on the same viral genome.
Low-frequency observations may be affected by amplification, sequencing errors, and read depth, while sampling frequency and quality may vary across locations and time.

Methods developed for complete individual-level genomes therefore cannot be applied directly to wastewater sequencing data without additional genome reconstruction steps [27, 28], which introduce considerable uncertainty and computational complexity.
text.formatted: Methods developed for complete individual-level genomes therefore cannot be applied directly to wastewater sequencing data without additional genome reconstruction steps <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref>, which introduce considerable uncertainty and computational complexity.

text.text: A simpler approach to analyzing wastewater sequence data is to compare mutation profiles without reconstructing linkage between mutations.
Related mutation-based approaches have previously been used in clinical genomic epidemiology to estimate epidemiological parameters [29] and infer transmission routes [30].
text.formatted: Related mutation-based approaches have previously been used in clinical genomic epidemiology to estimate epidemiological parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> and infer transmission routes <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: More recently, mutation-based approaches have been applied to wastewater sequencing data to characterize genetic diversity and spatiotemporal patterns of viral variation [31, 32, 33].
text.formatted: More recently, mutation-based approaches have been applied to wastewater sequencing data to characterize genetic diversity and spatiotemporal patterns of viral variation <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33]</ref>.

text.text: Although these studies demonstrate that mutation profiles capture meaningful temporal and geographic patterns, they do not directly evaluate how accurately mutation-based similarity recovers underlying transmission structure.

Furthermore, while genetic similarity has been shown to correlate with geographic proximity [33], its relationship to independent measures of epidemiological connectivity, such as human mobility data, remains underexplored.
text.formatted: Furthermore, while genetic similarity has been shown to correlate with geographic proximity <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>, its relationship to independent measures of epidemiological connectivity, such as human mobility data, remains underexplored.

text.text: To address this gap, we develop interpretable mutation-counting methods that translate spatiotemporal patterns of wastewater mutations into estimated transmission matrices (ETMs, see Fig. 1).
text.formatted: To address this gap, we develop interpretable mutation-counting methods that translate spatiotemporal patterns of wastewater mutations into estimated transmission matrices (ETMs, see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: We establish using epidemic simulations that these estimated matrices recover spatial transmission structure under realistic 2 . observation limits.

We then apply the approach to wastewater surveillance data from Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, revealing seasonal reorganization of spatial transmission patterns in agreement with expectations from mobility data.

By focusing on the differences between the estimated matrices and mobility, we detect location-specific deviations coinciding with regional interventions, and temporal variation in crossborder connectivity.
Through these results, we demonstrate the untapped potential of wastewater sequence data as a complementary tool for monitoring realized patterns of spatial disease transmission.
Wastewater data from Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein were harmonized by wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) catchment and sampling week (Methods 1.1).
The Austrian dataset, which also included samples from Liechtenstein, comprised 6,534 samples collected between January 2021 and December 2024 from 48 catchments.
The Swiss dataset included 1,371 samples collected between May 2021 and August 2024 from 15 catchments.
We also developed an end-to-end synthetic validation pipeline to reproduce the main steps of the data generation and observation process (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: We also developed an end-to-end synthetic validation pipeline to reproduce the main steps of the data generation and observation process (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The pipeline combined spatial contact network generation, an individual-based epidemic and mutation simulation, and a synthetic wastewater observation model with a soft allele-frequency detection limit (Methods 1.3).

Both the empirical and the synthetic pipelines produced the same type of output: whether a particular substitution was observed at a given time and location, allowing the same inference methods to be evaluated in simulations and applied to empirical data.
These observations were converted into ETMs, which aim to approximate the true transmission matrix between locations, up to scaling factors.
We propose two complementary methods for inferring ETMs, illustrated in Fig. 2a.
text.formatted: We propose two complementary methods for inferring ETMs, illustrated in Fig. <ref type="figure">2a</ref>.

text.text: We call the first approach First-Occurrence Propagation (FOP) counting, as it identifies mutations that are first observed in a single location and records their subsequent appearance at other locations at the next observation time as directed, one-step propagation events.
FOP counting can be shown theoretically to be proportional to the true directed transmission counts under idealized transmission and observation models (Supplementary Section G).
Its main limitation is that newly arising mutations may initially be carried by only a single infected individual.
FOP counting therefore requires highly sensitive mutation detection and becomes less reliable when low-frequency mutations are missed.
We propose Co-occurrence Adjusted for Prevalence (CAP) counting as a more robust alternative to FOP counting.
At each time point, it measures the mutations shared by each pair of locations and weights each mutation inversely by the number of locations in which it is observed.
Mutations confined to a small number of locations therefore contribute more than widespread mutations, which provide little information about specific connections.
CAP counting is a heuristic and does not infer direction, but it uses all informative shared mutations rather than only first-observation events.

Together with the preserved spatial structure, these results demonstrate the potential of ETMs for cross-border transmission analysis, particularly as wastewater surveillance protocols become more standardized across countries.

We showed that spatiotemporal mutation observations from pooled wastewater samples can be used to infer estimated transmission matrices that retain information about the spatial structure of an epidemic.
To estimate these matrices we introduced two interpretable mutation-counting approaches, FOP and CAP counting, and evaluated them extensively in simulation analyses.
FOP counting uses the sequential appearance of mutations to estimate directed connections and has a direct theoretical relationship to transmission under idealized conditions.
CAP counting measures prevalence-adjusted mutation co-occurrence and is symmetric, but recovered the known transmission matrices more reliably under realistic observation limits.

We therefore used CAP counting for the main empirical analyses to compare transmission structure inferred from genetic sequences with independent mobility data, examining both broad similarities and location-specific differences.
Several of our results point to similarities between the inferred transmission structure and independent measures of population movement.
In Austria, the effective distance-decay exponent varied seasonally and was correlated with temporal Google and Meta mobility indicators.
We note that while the correlation of the mobility measures and the distance-decay exponent is reassuring, their comparison is inherently indirect.

A more direct comparison was possible in the United States, where spatiotemporal SafeGraph mobility matrices were available, and the distance-decay exponent of the mobility matrices could also be computed.

Although this analysis used clinical sequences aggregated to resemble wastewater observations, the high correlation between the distance-decay exponents of the two datasets indicates similar temporal variation in their spatial localization.

At the international scale, the Austria-Switzerland cross-border connectivity multiplier also varied similarly to bilateral overnight stays, including a marked decrease during winter and spring 2021-2022.
These comparisons show that ETMs recover spatial and temporal patterns that are also present in independent mobility data.
Differences between ETMs and mobility networks may be particularly informative, as they can identify locations where routine movement does not translate into transmission as expected.
Their interpretation, however, depends on the mobility dataset used for comparison.

For Austria, we compared the ETMs with a static post-pandemic commuting matrix, which captures routine work-related mobility but not the temporal changes in movement and behaviour observed during the study period.

The patterns involving Vienna, Vorarlberg and Innsbruck coincided with documented changes in restrictions, reopening and seasonal tourism, although these associations do not establish a causal explanation.

Spatiotemporal mobility networks would allow finer comparisons and could help distinguish changes in movement from other factors affecting transmission, such as regional immunity, contact behaviour or susceptibility.
However, even spatiotemporal mobility datasets have important limitations.

Mobile-device and platform data may represent only selected population groups or types of movement, and even detailed movement records do not measure the specific encounters through which infections spread.

ETMs and mobility networks should therefore be viewed as complementary: mobility data describe selected opportunities for movement and contact, whereas ETMs summarize the spatial structure reflected in the similarity of pathogen genetic variation.
The population-pooled nature of wastewater surveillance also creates opportunities for cross-border analyses.

Wastewater sampling is less dependent than clinical surveillance on individual testing behaviour and access to healthcare, and similar measurements can be collected independently in neighbouring countries.
By combining Austrian and Swiss wastewater data, we constructed a joint ETM whose temporal variation was consistent with bilateral overnight-stay data.
Such analyses are nevertheless difficult because national surveillance programs can differ in sampling density, laboratory procedures, sequencing equipment and detection sensitivity.
Interlaboratory comparisons have similarly shown that wastewater variant detection depends on adequate sequencing coverage and continued quality control [47].

text.text: These differences may have contributed to Liechtenstein appearing more closely connected to Austrian than to Swiss catchments in our analysis.
Despite these limitations, the recovery of coherent cross-border structure from independently generated national datasets shows the potential of coordinated international wastewater surveillance.
Several additional limitations affect the interpretation of the inferred matrices.
CAP counting is symmetric and cannot determine the direction of movement or transmission.
Its performance also depends on dense, repeated and sufficiently comparable sequencing across locations and time.
Although we assessed sensitivity to missing catchment-time reports (Supplementary Fig.
A.3h), repeated introductions from outside the sampled region or a systematic lack of observations from highly connected catchments could still bias inferred connectivity.
The simulations also showed that the distance-decay exponent fitted to an ETM was attenuated relative to the exponent of the generating contact matrix.
The fitted β eff should therefore be interpreted as a comparative measure of spatial localization rather than as an unbiased estimate of the underlying contact process.
Furthermore, broad transmission structure was recovered more reliably than local deviations, with FOP counting sometimes outperforming CAP counting for detecting localized changes.
Future estimators could improve CAP counting by incorporating some of the temporal information recovered by FOP counting.
The interpretation of the empirical results has additional limitations: comparisons depend on the mobility data available, and associations with policies or travel activity remain observational.
Finally, the current analyses are largely restricted to SARS-CoV-2, for which unusually extensive longitudinal sequencing data are available.
Future work should apply these methods to additional pathogens, geographic settings and intervention periods.

In particular, combining harmonized wastewater sequencing with detailed spatiotemporal mobility networks could reveal new biological and public-health insights into when transmission follows standard mobility patterns and when it is altered by interventions, behavioural changes, immunity or administrative borders.

Our results therefore support extending coordinated wastewater sequencing within and across countries as a new source of information on spatial epidemic spread, especially when direct observations of transmission are unavailable.

We quantified relationships between locations using two proposed matrix-based measures, FOP counting and CAP counting, and temporally resolved Jaccard similarity as a baseline.
All three measures were calculated from observations (m, t, i) indicating that mutation m was observed at time t in location i.
Matrices used a common set of K locations and had zero diagonal entries.
FOP counting records directed one-step temporal propagation.
For each mutation m, we determined its first observed time t 0 (m) and retained it only when it was first observed in exactly one source location, s(m).
At the next global observation time, t 1 (m), the mutation contributed a directed event s(m) → j for every other location j in which it was observed.
Let c ij (t) be the number of such events from source i to target j whose target time is t.

To account for incomplete reporting, we defined O ij as the set of consecutive-time observation opportunities for which source i was represented at the preceding global time point and target j was represented at time t.
The FOP counting score was with M FOP ij = 0 when O ij was empty or no propagation event was observed.
Observation opportunities with no event contributed zero.
FOP counting is directed; target locations index matrix rows and source locations index columns.

Figure1: Conceptual framework for estimating and evaluating ETMs.
Contact patterns between locations give rise to realized transmission through epidemic spread, which is reflected in pathogen genetic variation.
Wastewater sequencing provides an incomplete observation of this variation because of withincatchment mixing, incomplete sampling and detection limits.
We infer estimated transmission matrices (ETMs) from these wastewater mutation observations.
In synthetic experiments, ETMs can be compared directly with the known realized transmission matrix and underlying contact structure.

In empirical data, ETMs are compared with independent mobility and commuting data to identify both broad similarities in spatial transmission structure and departures from mobility-based expectations.
